🪙 A COUPLE WALKING THEIR DOG FOUND $10 MILLION IN BURIED GOLD

In February 2013, a couple known only as John and Mary were walking their dog on their rural Northern California property when they spotted a rusty metal can poking out of the dirt.

The can was so heavy they thought it held old paint. On the walk home its lid cracked open, revealing the edge of a gold coin. They went back with hand tools, and later a metal detector, and eventually dug up eight cans holding 1,427 gold coins dated 1847 to 1894.

Most were $20 Liberty Head double eagles struck at the San Francisco Mint. The face value was $27,980, but the coin firm Kagin's estimated the hoard's market value at more than $10 million. It is considered the largest find of buried gold coins ever made in the United States.

Nobody knows who buried it. The couple nicknamed the spot Saddle Ridge.

⭐️ SEC eyes enforcement action over prediction market insider trading 

🔖 The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has warned that prediction markets offering contracts linked to corporate earnings and business performance could face enforcement action over insider trading, fraud and market manipulation. SEC Enforcement Director David Woodcock said the agency was monitoring activity on prediction platforms and expected to pursue potential securities violations. He added that enforcement activity was likely “in the future, for sure,” although he did not identify a particular company or announce new charges.

➡️ Woodcock’s comments centered on contracts that allow traders to bet on financial results or key performance indicators, commonly known as KPIs. Such products can involve outcomes tied to quarterly earnings, sales figures or other measures of a listed company’s business performance. The SEC oversees securities markets, while the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) regulates many derivatives contracts. Prediction markets can raise questions about which agency has authority when a contract’s outcome depends on a publicly traded company.

🔔 The regulator has already approved a Cboe Global Markets proposal involving binary options tied to corporate performance measures. The contracts allow traders to take positions on outcomes such as Citigroup’s earnings per share or Apple’s iPhone sales revenue. The decision addressed Cboe’s particular products and did not establish that every prediction contract involving a company’s performance automatically falls under SEC jurisdiction.

The eighth survival rule.

Bolting the door and stockpiling food in the living room does not make your home a safe fortress. Most people who lost their lives inside their homes during the Bosnian War and hurricane disasters did so because they did not know 'how to fortify a home.'

Five ironclad rules of home defense for avoiding becoming a target for looters and protecting your family and shelter to the very end.

1. Blind faith in door locks and front doors: Doors are breached through the 'door frame.'

Even the latest digital door locks or auxiliary locks can be ripped off in 15 seconds with a single steel pry bar (crowbar). Looters do not pick the lock; they use a pry bar to break the door hinges and door frame (strike plate) and force their way in.
The key to protecting your door is not an expensive lock, but long steel screws at least 7.5 cm long that anchor the door frame deep into the wall, and a steel security bar placed under the door.

2. Lights at night are 'lighthouses' that attract snipers and looters.

A city without power is pitch-black at night. In those conditions, a single candle or the glow of a smartphone screen in the living room can cast your silhouette through the curtains for up to 1 km.
It is effectively advertising to the entire neighborhood: "This house still has batteries, candles, and supplies."
At night, cover windows completely with aluminum foil emergency blankets or blackout tape to achieve 100% blackout, and use only red light or a tiny lantern pointed at the floor.

3. Cooking smells are 'pheromones' that turn hungry neighbors into looters.

After 4–5 days without electricity and with grocery stores stripped bare, people become extremely sensitive to hunger.
At that point, the smell of meat cooking or warm instant noodles boiling in the kitchen spreads throughout the building through vents and hallways.
The moment they catch the scent, even a neighbor who was normally kind becomes an intruder knocking on your door to survive. For the first 1–2 weeks of a crisis, you must get by without cooking or making any smells, using non-heated food (peanut butter, energy bars, canned food eaten cold).

4. The trap of standing watch by the window: Do not stand guard; become a 'shadow.'

Standing by a window with a gun or blunt weapon, looking outside, is not vigilance—it is suicide.
From outside, your head and shoulder silhouette against the window frame is clearly visible in the darkness. You become a perfect target for rocks or gunfire.
Do not observe the outside from right beside the window. Instead, stay behind a dark corner farther inside the room and look out at an angle, or use a small mirror to keep your body hidden while maintaining a view.

5. No protection against arson: A fortress without a fire extinguisher is a 'wood-burning stove.'

If an intruder cannot break through the door, what is the easiest tactic they can use? Setting fire to the ground floor, beneath the front door, or on the balcony.
No matter how impenetrable a fortress you build, once it fills with smoke and toxic gases, you will have to crawl out within 10 minutes.
Fortifying a home without a dry chemical fire extinguisher in every room, a gas mask with a filter cartridge, wet towels, and an escape rope is like trapping yourself in a mousetrap. You must secure an escape route at the back (a rear window or the roof).

Conclusion:
The safest home against looters is not an 'impenetrable steel fortress.'
It is one disguised as an 'empty house whose door has already been broken down and looted, making it look like there is nothing left worth taking.'
The greatest defense is not winning a fight, but never catching their eye in the first place.

Alphabet was the first to plunge, losing about 13% and nearly $500 billion in market value following its earnings report, before continuing to slide the next day. Then Intel crashed by roughly 29%, even though its Data Center and AI division grew by 78%.

Taken together, these two stories look much more interesting than just two bad days for tech companies.

At Google, AI is growing at a breakneck pace, but the company has posted negative free cash flow for the second consecutive quarter. At Intel, demand for server solutions is enormous, but at the same time, the AI boom is draining memory supplies and manufacturing capacity away from the traditional PC market, which remains critical to the company. As a result, one of the biggest beneficiaries of AI is beginning to suffer from the consequences of the race itself.

And this raises a much more important question. Could this be the moment when the market finally stops focusing solely on AI growth rates and starts calculating how much this entire revolution actually costs?

Until now, the weak points of the AI race have mostly existed somewhere in the forecasts. 
Everyone understood that data centers cost enormous amounts of money, resources were in short supply, and returns on these investments would take time to materialize. Now, in just two days, the market has been given two very expensive demonstrations of these risks involving some of the world's largest tech companies.

And this could genuinely become dangerous for the entire market. That's because a significant portion of the S&P 500 and Nasdaq's growth over the past few years has been driven precisely by a handful of the largest tech companies and expectations surrounding AI. If the market starts reassessing how much Google, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, Nvidia, and the rest should be worth in light of the actual cost of the AI race, we will be talking about much more than a correction in individual stocks.

At that point, the main question will no longer be which company is next. The real question will be how far the entire market could fall if the biggest driver of its growth in recent years suddenly becomes its biggest source of valuation risk.
